items.title: Can DRTs accept written statements after 45 days? Delhi, Telangana and P&H High Courts differ
items.summary: The Delhi High Court has held that Debts Recovery Tribunals (DRTs) cannot accept written statements beyond 45 days under the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act [Nikhil Podar Vs PNB]. However, the Telangana High Court and the Punjab and Haryana High Court have taken the opposite view. A Division Bench of Justices Subramonium Prasad and Renu Bhatnagar of Delhi High Court held that the 30-day period prescribed for filing a written statement can be extended by a maximum of 15 days, and that courts have no power to condone any further delay. “ The delay beyond the maximum period 45 days prescribed under Section 19(5)(i) of the RDB Act cannot be condoned by any Court," the Court said. Justice Subramonium Prasad The Court was hearing a petition filed by Nikhil Poddar against a Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT) order refusing to take his written statement on record in recovery proceedings initiated by Punjab National Bank. Poddar's counsel received the complete pleadings/ paper book on September 6, 2019. The written statement was filed on November 26, beyond the 45-day period. items.title: Low IQ or intellectual disability alone won't make an accused unfit to stand trial: Kerala High Court
items.summary: The Kerala High Court recently held that low intelligence quotient (IQ) or an intellectual disability alone is not enough to declare that an accused is incapable of defending themselves before a court or unfit to stand trial. [Kamal Raj v State of Kerala] Justice Jobin Sebastian explained that Section 368 the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) lays down the procedure to be followed in case a person of unsound mind is tried before court. Under this provision, courts are required to enquire into the accused person's mental condition, their capacity to defend themselves and to postpone criminal proceedings if they are found incapable of making their defence. The Court stated that the important issue to be considered is whether the mental condition or disability prevents the accused from understanding the nature of the proceedings, whether they can understand the questions put to them and communicate the necessary facts and instructions to their lawyer. " The mere presence of an intellectual disability or a low IQ, by itself, will not make a person incapacitated to stand trial, " the Court said. items.title: ‘Repeatedly erased’: Trans filmmaker flags misgendering, non-inclusivity at IDSFFK
items.summary: When trans non-binary filmmaker Harshappi Harsh (they/them) arrived at the 18th International Documentary and Short Film Festival of Kerala (IDSFFK) as a guest filmmaker, they expected to screen their film, meet fellow filmmakers, and spend time with friends. Instead, they said they spent much of the festival correcting people who repeatedly misgendered them, looking for a toilet they could comfortably use, and raising concerns about a lack of inclusivity at the festival. Harshappi, a transmasculine non-binary photographer, filmmaker, and community organiser from Thiruvananthapuram, had their 20-minute documentary To Stitch Together a Watermelon Heart selected for the short documentary competition at the festival. The film, which is based on Harshappi’s own experiences, explores their journey as a trans non-binary person and questions the erasure of trans and queer experiences. But Harshappi’s own experience at the festival left them feeling repeatedly erased. “I came here with my film to enjoy some time with my friends and showcase my work.
